**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 64, verses 5–7:**

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿Has there not come to you the news of those who disbelieved before? So they tasted the bad consequence of their affair, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿That is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, and they said, "Shall mere humans guide us?" So they disbelieved and turned away, and Allah was self-sufficient. And Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved claim that they will never be resurrected. Say, "Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected; then you will surely be informed of what you did. And that is easy for Allah."﴾

"ألَمْ يَأْتِكُمْ" is in the jazm (the jussive mood, apocopation). Its original form is "يَأْتِيكُمْ". Sibawayh said: "Know that the one that is quiescent in the raf' (nominative) case is elided in the jazm case." The address in this verse is to Quraysh. They were told of what befell 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and others whose news Quraysh had heard. "Wabal al-amr" means its disliked outcome and what harms a person from it.

Allah's saying "dhalika bi-annahu" refers to tasting the bad consequence and to the punishment of the Hereafter being theirs. Then Allah mentioned, from the statements of those earlier peoples, what resembles the statements of the disbelievers of Quraysh: their denial that Allah would send a human being as a messenger, their denial that any of the children of Adam could be a prophet, and their envy of the one who was sent. In "أبَشَرٌ" the word is in the nominative as the subject of an inceptive sentence. The plural pronoun in "يَهْدُونَنا" is used because "al-bashar" is the name of this human species, as if they had said: "Are people our guides?"

Allah's saying "wa-istaghna Allah" is an expression for what became evident of their destruction and that they would never harm Allah in any way. Thus it became clear that He was self-sufficient from the beginning. Because their destruction became evident after it had not been evident, it is acceptable to use this self-sufficiency attributed to the Name of Allah, since the form "istaf'ala" is used for seeking a thing and obtaining it by seeking.

Allah's saying "Zanna alladhina kafaru" specifically addresses Quraysh, and then it also includes every disbeliever in resurrection. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Al-za'm is the kunya of falsehood." The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ)) said: "Wretched is the mount of a man: 'they claim'." "Za'ama" is not used in eloquent speech except as an expression for falsehood, or for a statement that its speaker alone holds, so the transmitter wishes to place the responsibility for it upon the one who claims it. In this there is an indication that inclines toward weakening the claim. Sibawayh's saying "Za'ama al-Khalil" is used only for what al-Khalil alone holds.

Then Allah commanded him (ﷺ) to answer their denial with what requires a rebuttal of them and an affirmation of resurrection, and to confirm that with an oath. Finally, at the end of the verse, He threatened them that they would be informed of their deeds, in the manner of reproach and rebuke that leads to punishment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 64, verses 12–15:

The Exalted One's saying:

﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger. But if you turn away, then upon Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance.﴾ ﴿Allah – there is no deity except Him. And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. But if you pardon and overlook and forgive, then indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Your wealth and your children are but a trial, and Allah has with Him a great reward.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: "wa-aṭī'ū" (and obey) is conjoined (ʿuṭifa) to His saying "fa-āminū" (so believe), and His saying, glorified is He, "fa-in tawallaytum" (but if you turn away) to the end of the verse is a warning (waʿīd) and an absolving of Muhammad (ﷺ) once he has conveyed the message. In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely⁠﴾ is an exhortation to the believers to strive against the disbelievers and to be patient upon the religion of Allah, exalted is He.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them⁠﴾ to the end of the surah is a Medinan (madanī) revelation. The people differed concerning its occasion of revelation. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: it was revealed concerning ʿAwf ibn Mālik al-Ashjaʿī, because he intended to join a military expedition (ghazw) with the Prophet (ﷺ), but his family and children gathered around him, discouraged him, and complained to him about being separated from them, so he did not go out. Then he regretted it and intended to punish them, so the verse was revealed concerning him, warning against spouses and children and their trial. Then Allah, exalted is He, turned him away from punishing them with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿But if you pardon and overlook and forgive⁠﴾.

Some exegetes (mufassirūn) said: the occasion of the verse is that some people believed in Allah, exalted is He, but their spouses and children discouraged them from emigration (hijrah), so they did not emigrate until after a period of time. Then they found that others had gained understanding (tafaqquh) in the religion, so they regretted, grieved, and intended to punish their spouses and children.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that wealth and children are a trial (fitnah) that preoccupies a person from his right guidance, and carries him, through desire for this world, to what does not please him in his Hereafter. From this is His (ﷺ) saying: "The child is a cause of miserliness and a cause of cowardice." Abū Dāwūd recorded in his Musannaf a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was delivering the khutbah on Friday when al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, came, wearing two red shirts, dragging them, stumbling and getting up. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) descended from the minbar, took them both, brought them up with him, then recited this verse and said: 'I saw these two and I could not be patient,' then resumed his khutbah."

The Qadi Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These and similar things are the trial of the virtuous (fuḍalāʾ). As for the trial of the ignorant and the sinful (fasaqah), it leads to every destruction. Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "None of you should say: 'O Allah, protect me from trial,' for no one returns to his family and wealth without being involved in trial. Rather, let him say: 'O Allah, I seek refuge in You from misleading trials.'" ʿUmar said to Ḥudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with them both: "How have you woken up?" He said: "I have woken up loving trial and hating the truth." ʿUmar said: "What is this?" He said: "I love my child and I hate death."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has with Him a great reward⁠﴾ is a discouragement from this world and an encouragement toward the Hereafter.

And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. (p. 324) Qatada and a group of people said: His words, exalted is He, ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ abrogate His words, ﴿Fear Allah with the fear that is due to Him﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:102]. It was narrated that the command to fear Allah with the fear that is due to Him was hard on the people, until ﴿as much as you are able﴾ was revealed. A group among them, including Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas, held that there is no abrogation (naskh, the cancelling of one ruling by a later one) in the two verses. They said that His words, ﴿with the fear that is due to Him﴾, mean ﴿as much as you are able﴾. No one can be commanded to obey beyond his capacity and ability, so on this interpretation the latter verse clarifies the former. This verse may also mean: fear Allah for as long as you are able to be mindful of Him, so that "mā" (ما) is a temporal particle covering the whole span of time, as if He said: "your life, and for as long as action is possible."

His words, exalted is He, ﴿khayran﴾ ("good"). Some grammarians held that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), but this is weak. Others held that it is governed by His words, "and spend" (أنفقوا), and they said that the predicate here is wealth. Yet another group held that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, its implied form being "spending that is good" (إنفاقًا خيرًا). The view of Sibawayh is that it is in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by "spend" (أنفقوا).

Abu Haywa read "yuwaqqa" (يُوَقَّ) with a fatha on the waw and a shadda on the qaf. Abu 'Amr, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "shiḥḥa" (شِحَّ) with a kasra on the shin. Its explanation has already been given in Surat al-Hashr. Al-Hasan said: "Your looking at a woman you do not possess is a form of stinginess (shuḥḥ)." It was also said: "O Messenger of Allah, what causes a servant to enter the Fire?" He (ﷺ) said: "When you see obeyed stinginess, followed desire, and every person of opinion pleased with his own opinion, then hold fast to what is peculiar to yourself."

The majority of the seven readers read "yuḍā'ifuhu" (يُضاعِفُهُ). Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "yuḍā'ifuhu" (يُضاعِفُهُ) with the vowelling as recorded in the mushaf. (p. 325) Some scholars held that this urging is to pay the obligatory zakat. Others held that the verse concerns what is recommended (mandūb), and this is the more correct view, if Allah the Exalted wills.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿and Allah is Most Appreciative﴾ is a report of His recompense.

Upon the thing, and that He removes it from whomever Allah wills. The Mighty, there is no lord besides Him.

The commentary on Surat al-Taghabun is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
